title: Migrating Legacy Division
learning_outcomes: Explain migrating legacy division and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply migrating legacy division in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Migrating Legacy Division** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect identifying division expressions with understanding slash-separated css syntax, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: SassScript evaluates expressions while compiling. Use explicit parentheses for order, compatible units for arithmetic, and interpolation only where a value must become part of a selector, property name, or string.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Modern CSS uses slash syntax in several properties, so do not assume every slash is Sass division. Use `sass:math` and `math.div()` where arithmetic is intended, then check the emitted CSS.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Audit a small stylesheet for migrating legacy division. Save the original source and compiled CSS, make one deliberate change, recompile, and write down the evidence that the change is correct and safe.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
